title: 1907 Panic — going long in the pit at the bottom
statement: During the banking panic of 1907, Livermore recognized that forced liquidation had exhausted itself and bought stocks at distressed prices while other traders were being wiped out.
outcome: He made his first million-dollar profit; J.P. Morgan himself reportedly sent word asking him to stop shorting (which Livermore had already stopped). The trade made his national reputation at age 30.

title: 1929 crash — shorting the greatest bull market in history
statement: Recognizing classic distribution signs — leadership stalling, volume rising on declines, brokers' loans swelling — Livermore built a massive short position across leading stocks into October 1929.
outcome: On Black Tuesday and the days after, his reported profit reached $100 million, roughly $1.5 billion in modern terms. It was the greatest single trade of his career and the peak of his wealth.

title: 1908 cotton trade — trusting a tip against his own system
statement: Livermore violated his own rules by averaging down in cotton on the advice of Ted Pahle, a trader he trusted, adding to a losing position until the loss consumed his entire capital.
outcome: He went broke for the third time and famously said the loss of money was nothing next to the lesson: never average losses, never trade on another man's judgment. The episode is a canonical case study in discipline failure.

title: The pivotal points system — trading only at confirmation
statement: Livermore distilled his tape-reading into explicit rules: wait for pivotal points — price levels where a stock confirms or refutes its trend — and never act before confirmation, never anticipate the market.
outcome: The pivotal-point doctrine, published in his 1940 book 'How to Trade in Stocks,' anticipated modern breakout trading and remains the intellectual ancestor of trend-following systems.

title: Bucket-shop apprenticeship — learning to read the tape
statement: At 14, Livermore took a job posting quotes at Paine Webber's Boston office and taught himself to recognize repeating patterns in the ticker, testing predictions in bucket shops where bets were placed on price moves.
outcome: He became so consistently profitable that Boston bucket shops banned him; by his early twenties 'The Boy Plunger' had banked his first $10,000 stake trading on pattern recognition alone.

title: 1915 return from bankruptcy with Bethlehem Steel
statement: Owing over $1 million after the 1914 failure, Livermore rebuilt discipline in a small office, waiting weeks for the right setup before buying Bethlehem Steel on war demand at the pivotal point — his first position of size since his comeback.
outcome: The trade roughly quintupled his stake, paid off all his old debts in full — though he was not legally obliged to after bankruptcy — and restored his standing in Wall Street.
